intro:
By the end of this track you can model data the way modern Java intends. Picture the paperwork at a small town library: a loan slip in a clear sleeve, a request form with a fixed set of boxes to tick, a clerk who reads each form in one look, and a clerk at the door who checks everything that arrives from outside. Records, sealed types, pattern switches and data-oriented design are those four pictures in code. You'll know where each promise stops (shallow immutability, `null`, a subtype added after compilation), and you can say, with versions, what Project Valhalla has and hasn't shipped. Every lesson sets the Java feature next to its Kotlin counterpart, from data classes and sealed interfaces to `when` with guards and `@JvmInline value class`, and says plainly which side is better at what.

You need only the syntax of both languages; the track starts from zero on records and sealed types. Install JDK 25. Records, sealed types, pattern switches and record patterns are all final in JDK 21, so the labs compile with `--release 21`. Anything newer is marked with its JDK: unnamed patterns (`_`) need JDK 22, flexible constructor bodies JDK 25, primitive patterns are still a preview, and value objects exist only as a preview in early-access builds of JDK 28.

The labs live in `labs/modernjava`, one package per lesson (`workbench.modernjava.l01` to `l04`), and they all use the library: its forms as records, its items as a sealed type, its loan rules as one switch, and a reply from the regional catalogue parsed into a closed model. Lessons 1 to 3 are in Java and lesson 4 is in Kotlin. Two of the lesson 2 tests run `javac` inside the test through `javax.tools`, so Gradle must run on a full JDK. Run `./gradlew :modernjava:test --tests 'workbench.modernjava.lNN.*'` from `labs/` until it passes, and `./gradlew :modernjava:solutionTest` to run the same tests on the reference answers. Demos for newer JDKs sit in `labs/modernjava/preview` (run them with `java preview/File.java`), and two compile-it-yourself experiments sit in `labs/modernjava/javac`.
cheatsheet:
## Which JDK has what

| Feature | Status |
|---|---|
| Records (JEP 395) | final since JDK 16 |
| Sealed classes and interfaces (JEP 409) | final since JDK 17 |
| `instanceof` patterns (JEP 394) | final since JDK 16 |
| Pattern `switch`, `case null`, guards (JEP 441) | final since JDK 21 |
| Record patterns (JEP 440) | final since JDK 21 |
| Unnamed variables and patterns, `_` | preview in 21, final from JDK 22 |
| Flexible constructor bodies (statements before `this(...)`) | final from JDK 25 |
| Primitive types in patterns | preview in every JDK from 23 to 27, still preview |
| Derived record creation, `r with { ... }` (JEP 468) | Candidate JEP, on hold, in no JDK |
| Value objects, `value record` (JEP 401) | preview in JDK 28 (early-access builds now, release scheduled for March 2027) |
| "missing patterns:" list in exhaustiveness errors | javac from JDK 27 |

Final means finished and switched on. Preview means switched off unless you pass `--enable-preview`, and still open to change, so previews stay out of the labs.

## Picture it: the library's paperwork

| Idea | In code | Picture it |
|---|---|---|
| Record | `record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf)` | a filled-in form in a clear sleeve: what you see is all there is |
| Compact constructor | `Shelfmark { ... }` | the clerk at the counter who checks every form, whichever door it came through |
| Shallow immutability | a `List` component | a list stapled behind the form, which its owner can still write on |
| Wither, `copy()` | `withDue(...)`, `copy(days = 35)` | fill in a new form; it passes the counter again |
| Sealed type | `sealed interface LibraryItem permits ...` | a form with a fixed set of boxes to tick |
| `non-sealed` branch | `non-sealed interface PartnerItem` | the box "From another library: ______", with a blank line after it |
| Exhaustive switch | a switch with no `default` | the clerk's sheet has one line per box, and the compiler checks it |
| Record pattern | `Loan(Member(var id, int age), Book b, var branch)` | reading several boxes, and a form clipped inside, in one look |
| Guards and order | `case Book b when b.newRelease()` | the sheet is read from the top; the first line that fits wins |
| Remainder, `MatchException` | an old jar meets a new subtype | a form printed after the clerk's sheet was written |
| Parse at the edge | `parse(raw)` returns `Ok` or `Rejected` | the clerk at the door copies each letter onto the right form, or sends it back |
| Value object (JDK 28 preview) | `value record Shelf(short floor, short row)` | a form printed straight onto the page, with no envelope |

Where the pictures break: a list stapled to a paper form can't be someone else's list that keeps growing, but a record's `List` component can. A real clerk would ask a colleague about an unknown form, while a switch throws `MatchException`. And with value objects, the JVM, not you, decides what gets printed onto the page, and only small forms qualify.

## Records

```java
public record Shelfmark(String section, int shelf) {
    public Shelfmark {                                          // compact canonical constructor
        Objects.requireNonNull(section, "section");
        section = section.trim().toUpperCase(Locale.ROOT);       // reassign the parameter
        if (shelf < 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("shelf must be 1 or more");
    }                                                           // javac assigns the fields here
    public Shelfmark withShelf(int s) { return new Shelfmark(section, s); }   // a wither
}
record Crate(String branch, List<String> titles) { Crate { titles = List.copyOf(titles); } }   // defensive copy
```

```kotlin
data class Shelfmark(val section: String, val shelf: Int) {
    init { require(shelf >= 1) { "shelf must be 1 or more" } }      // runs on every construction and copy()
    companion object { fun of(section: String, shelf: Int) = Shelfmark(section.trim().uppercase(), shelf) }   // tidy here
}
val next = mark.copy(shelf = 13)                                    // generated, shallow, runs init
```

- Generated: private final fields, accessors (`section()`, no `get`), one canonical constructor, `equals`, `hashCode` and `toString`.
- No instance fields in the body, no `extends`. Static members, methods and nested types are fine. Eight component names are forbidden, `wait` among them.
- `equals` compares every component: `Objects.equals` for references, `compare` for primitives (`NaN` equals `NaN`, `0.0` doesn't equal `-0.0`). Arrays compare by reference.
- Shallow: copy `List`, `Set` and `Map` components with `copyOf`, or a changed list loses its record in a `HashSet`.
- The generated methods read fields, not accessors. To hide a phone number, override `toString`.
- Java deserialization runs a record's canonical constructor. It skips a Kotlin data class's `init`, unless the class is `@JvmRecord`.
- Records are identity objects: `==` compares references, `synchronized` works.

## Sealed types

| Subtype modifier | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `final` (records and enums already are) | no subtypes |
| `sealed ... permits ...` | a closed list one level down |
| `non-sealed` | open again; one case still covers the branch |

| Rule | Java | Kotlin |
|---|---|---|
| Where subtypes live | same module; on the class path, same package | same package and same module |
| The list | `permits`, or inferred from one source file | whatever is declared in that package and module |
| Concrete parent | possible, and it's a value of its own: make it abstract | a sealed class is always abstract |
| Enforced by | javac, and the JVM at load time (`PermittedSubclasses`) | kotlinc; with a JDK 17+ target, the same class-file attribute |

## Pattern switch

```java
return switch (loan) {
    case Loan(var m, Book(var format, var isNew), var b) when format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42;
    case Loan(var m, Book book, var b) -> 21;                // unguarded: closes the Book family
    case Loan(var m, Disc disc, var b) -> 7;
    case Loan(Member member, Magazine mag, var b) -> 7;
};                                                           // no default over a sealed type
```

```kotlin
return when (val item = loan.item) {
    is Book if item.format == Format.LARGE_PRINT -> 42      // guard: Kotlin 2.2+
    is Book -> 21
    is Disc -> 7
    is Magazine -> 7
}
```

- Cases run top to bottom; the first match wins. Guards never count toward exhaustiveness.
- A null selector throws `NullPointerException` unless there is `case null`. `default` doesn't catch null.
- A nested type pattern (`Point p`) matches a null component; a nested record pattern (`Point(var x, var y)`) doesn't.
- An old program meeting a subtype or enum constant added later throws `MatchException` (Kotlin: `NoWhenBranchMatchedException`).
- Several patterns in one arm only with `_`: `case Return _, Renew _ ->` (JDK 22+).
- Kotlin destructuring `val (a, b) = x` goes by position and swaps silently. kotlinc has no dominance check.

| javac says | It means |
|---|---|
| `the switch expression does not cover all possible input values` | a permitted subtype (or combination) has no unguarded case |
| `this case label is dominated by a preceding case label` | an earlier unguarded case already matches everything this one could |
| `illegal fall-through from a pattern` | several patterns with bindings in one arm |
| `class is not allowed to extend sealed class: X (as it is not listed in its 'permits' clause)` | a subtype missing from `permits` |
| `sealed, non-sealed or final modifiers expected` | a permitted subtype without its modifier |
| `class X in unnamed module cannot extend a sealed class in a different package` | split packages on the class path |

## Data-oriented design checklist

- One record per valid combination, under a sealed interface. No shared bag of nullable fields.
- Constructors refuse bad values; the type system refuses bad shapes.
- Parse untrusted input once, at the edge, into the model or a rejection. Trust the types behind the edge.
- The rules are functions with one exhaustive switch each. Keep methods for open, plug-in hierarchies and for behavior about the value itself.
- Don't depend on record identity, so `value` (JDK 28 preview) can be a one-word change later.
recap: A record is a final, transparent carrier, like a form in a clear sleeve: javac generates fields, accessors, one canonical constructor and the `Object` methods from the header, so they can't drift apart.

The compact constructor is the counter every instance passes: `new`, factories, other constructors, withers and Java deserialization all go through it. Kotlin's `init` is the twin, but it can't tidy a parameter, and Java deserialization skips it.
Records are only shallowly immutable and their generated methods read fields: copy collections with `copyOf`, and mask secrets in `toString`, not in the accessor.

A sealed type names its permitted subtypes, like a form with a fixed set of boxes; each one is final, sealed or non-sealed. On the class path they must share a package. A concrete sealed parent is a value of its own.
A switch over a sealed type with no default is checked by the compiler, so adding a subtype turns every forgotten switch into a compile error. A default hides it.
Record patterns read several boxes in one look. Cases run in order, guards don't count toward exhaustiveness, and javac rejects dominated cases, which kotlinc doesn't.
Exhaustive is a compile-time promise: null needs `case null`, and a subtype added after compilation makes an old switch throw `MatchException`.
Data-oriented code models closed data as records and sealed types, checks outside data at the edge, and writes the rules as functions. New operations are cheap and new types are loud.
Project Valhalla's value objects are a preview in JDK 28, not in 25 to 27. Records are identity objects; JEP 468 withers are on hold; null-restricted types are still drafts.

quiz.q: A `record MemberCard(String name, String phone)` is logged in full whenever a reservation fails. A teammate overrides `phone()` to return a masked value. What do the logs show now?
options: The masked number, because toString calls the accessor
The full number, because the generated toString reads the field
Nothing: overriding an accessor turns off the generated toString
A compile error: accessors can't be overridden
quiz.why: The generated `toString`, `equals` and `hashCode` get the private fields directly, so masking the accessor changes nothing in the logs and breaks the copy rule of `equals`. Override `toString` instead.

quiz.q: Which is the right place to turn `" fic "` into `"FIC"` so that no `Shelfmark` anywhere holds the raw value?
options: A static factory `Shelfmark.of`
The compact canonical constructor, by reassigning the parameter
The `section()` accessor
The code that reads the spine label
quiz.why: Every construction goes through the canonical constructor, including `new`, withers and Java deserialization. A factory can be bypassed with `new`, the accessor leaves the field raw (and `equals` compares fields), and the reading code covers only one entry point.

quiz.q: A Kotlin `data class PageRange(val first: Int, val last: Int) : Serializable` checks `first <= last` in `init`. A tampered Java-serialized stream says first = 5, last = 1. Which change makes deserialization reject it?
options: Mark the class `@JvmRecord`
Add `@Volatile` to both properties
Make the class `open`
Nothing can: Java deserialization never runs constructors
quiz.why: Java deserialization skips a plain data class's `init`, but a `@JvmRecord` data class is a real record, and records are rebuilt through their canonical constructor, so the check runs and the stream is rejected with `InvalidObjectException`.

quiz.q: Partner libraries must be able to add their own kinds of item in their own packages, while your switches over `LibraryItem` stay exhaustive with no default. How do you declare the partner branch?
options: `final class PartnerItem`
`sealed interface PartnerItem` with an empty permits list
`non-sealed interface PartnerItem extends LibraryItem`
Drop `sealed` from `LibraryItem` altogether
quiz.why: `non-sealed` reopens one branch to any class, and a single `case PartnerItem p` still covers every partner's implementation, so the switch stays exhaustive. Dropping `sealed` would lose exhaustiveness for every branch.

quiz.q: Your program runs on the class path. `sealed interface DeskEvent` is in `org.townlibrary.desk` and its records are in `org.townlibrary.desk.events`. What happens?
options: It compiles: the packages share a prefix
javac rejects it: in the unnamed module the permitted subtypes must be in the same package
It compiles, but the JVM won't load the records
It compiles only with fully qualified names in `permits`
quiz.why: Java packages have no hierarchy, so these are two unrelated packages. Without a named module javac reports that the class `cannot extend a sealed class in a different package`. Move the records, or put both packages in one module.

quiz.q: The cases are `case Book b when b.newRelease() -> 7;`, `case Book b when b.format() == LARGE_PRINT -> 42;`, `case Book b -> 21;`. What does javac do, and how many days does a new large-print book get?
options: javac rejects the second case as dominated; no loan
It compiles, and the book gets 42 days because the large-print rule is more specific
It compiles, and the book gets 7 days because the first matching case wins
javac rejects the switch as not exhaustive
quiz.why: Guarded cases never dominate, so javac accepts any order of them, and the switch is exhaustive thanks to the unguarded `case Book b`. At run time the first case whose pattern and guard both match wins: the new-release rule.

quiz.q: `case Line(Point(var x1, var y1), Point to) -> ...` is the only case of an exhaustive switch over `Line`. What happens for `new Line(null, new Point(1, 1))`?
options: The case matches with x1 and y1 left at 0
NullPointerException from the accessor
MatchException, because a nested record pattern never matches null
It doesn't compile: the switch isn't exhaustive
quiz.why: javac treats a null nested inside the selector as part of the remainder, so the switch compiles. At run time `Point(var x1, var y1)` doesn't match null, no case matches, and the switch throws `MatchException`. A type pattern `Point from` in that position would have matched the null.

quiz.q: A program was compiled against `enum Level { LOW, HIGH }` and switches over it with no default. It now runs next to a newer library where `Level` also has `CRITICAL`, and it gets `CRITICAL`. What happens?
options: The switch returns the value of its last case
MatchException
The JVM refuses to load the program's class
NullPointerException
quiz.why: An exhaustive switch over an enum, like one over a sealed type, has a hidden arm for values it didn't know at compile time, and that arm throws `MatchException`. Recompiling the program turns the gap into a compile error.

quiz.q: Every month the library asks for a new report over the same three kinds of account activity (borrowed, returned, renewed): overdue letters, a busiest-days chart, a yearly summary. Which design keeps each new report to one place?
options: A method per report on every activity class
A sealed interface of records, with each report as one function that switches over the activities
One class with a `type` string and nullable fields
A `default` branch in every switch for future kinds of activity
quiz.why: The operations grow and the types don't, so the data-oriented side of the expression problem wins: each report is a new function that touches no existing code. Methods on the classes would mean editing all three classes for every report.

quiz.q: Your team wants to mark `record Copy(long isbn13, int number)` as a `value record` for speed on the JDK 25 servers. What is accurate?
options: It works on JDK 25 with `--enable-preview`
Value objects are only a preview in JDK 28 builds; and a `long` plus an `int` is 64 bits or more of fields, which JDK 28 doesn't normally flatten anyway
Records are already value objects, so it changes nothing
It works on JDK 25, but only in Kotlin with `@JvmInline`
quiz.why: JEP 401 isn't in JDK 25, 26 or 27; it's a preview in JDK 28, which is still in development. Even there, flattened values must be read atomically and allow null, so values with 64 bits or more of field data aren't normally flattened. Kotlin's `@JvmInline value class` is a separate compile-time trick with one property.
